c1.story:
Stand at an Indraprastha Gas station in Delhi at six in the morning and watch the queue of auto-rickshaws, each waiting for a few kilos of CNG. The gas going into those tanks may have come out of an ONGC field off the east coast or off a tanker from Qatar. It travelled hundreds of kilometres through GAIL's steel pipe, then a few more under Delhi's roads through IGL's network, and ended up as fuel for the ride you are about to take to the metro.

Two very different businesses touched that molecule. The first owns the long-distance pipe. GAIL runs most of the national trunk network and Gujarat State Petronet covers Gujarat. They earn a tariff per unit carried, set by the regulator, much like a highway toll. GAIL also trades gas and makes petrochemicals, which adds a commodity swing on top of the toll.

The second owns the city. IGL in Delhi, Mahanagar Gas in Mumbai, Gujarat Gas across Gujarat and Adani Total Gas in dozens of newer areas each hold a licence to be the gas company for a geographic area. Inside that area, for years, they are effectively the only seller. They buy gas, partly at a cheap government-fixed price and partly at world prices, and sell it at a price they set themselves. For a long time that was one of the cosiest businesses on Dalal Street.

A city gas licence is a monopoly with a ration card. The monopoly is yours; the ration is Delhi's.

The ration card is the catch. The cheap domestic gas that made the margins fat is allotted by the petroleum ministry, and in late 2024 it cut that allotment in two steps to roughly half of what the distributors needed for CNG. Nothing changed in Delhi's traffic or Mumbai's kitchens. The stocks still fell by a third or more, because the market realised that a big part of the margin had been a policy gift, and gifts can be withdrawn.
c1.read:
Two tiles, two doors. Read each from top to bottom.

  • The name and the line under it say how each earns: the city distributor owns the pipes under a city and sets its own selling price; the trunk pipeline carries gas across states for a regulator-set tariff, with GAIL adding trading and petrochemicals.
  • The tickers are the listed names behind each door: IGL, MGL, ATGL and GUJGASLTD for the cities, GAIL and GSPL for the trunk lines. Click one to open its stock page.
  • The bar is how much of the profit the company keeps. Here is the counter-intuitive bit: the distributor sits at high and the pipeline at medium, even though the pipeline is the safer, more regulated business. The reason is that a regulator caps the pipeline's return, while the distributor sets its own price inside a monopoly. The high bar is exactly the margin the government reached in and trimmed in 2024.
  • The last line is the bet. Read the distributor's carefully: a bet on margin per unit, which the government can change overnight. That sentence is the whole risk.

The analogy underneath, the highway toll and the petrol pump at the end of it whose cheap tankers are rationed, maps neatly onto the tiles. The so-what then warns that one LNG headline can be good for one door and bad for the other. Try it: cheaper LNG lowers the distributor's cost but does little for the pipeline's toll, unless it brings new volume through the pipe.

c2.story:
Natural gas has an awkward life. It is invisible, it cannot be stored easily, and it has to travel through a sealed steel pipe or be chilled into a liquid, far colder than any freezer, and shipped. Gas is expensive to move, so the plumbing is the business.

The journey starts at the source. Some of India's gas comes from domestic fields: old ONGC and Oil India fields priced under a government formula, and newer deep-water fields in the Krishna-Godavari basin, including Reliance's, which get a premium price. The rest arrives as LNG, liquefied gas on ships from Qatar, the United States and Australia, at a world price.

The ships unload at terminals on the coast: Petronet at Dahej and Kochi, Shell at Hazira, GAIL at Dabhol, the Adani-Total venture at Dhamra on the east coast. The liquid is warmed back into gas and pushed into high-pressure trunk pipelines, mostly GAIL's, with GSPL's grid covering Gujarat. Then, at a city's edge, the pressure is stepped down and the gas enters the city network: compressed into CNG for vehicles, or piped under roads to kitchens and factories.

Why are Delhi and Mumbai the CNG cities? Because in 1998 the Supreme Court, hearing a public interest case on Delhi's choking air, ordered the city's buses and autos onto gas. The court built IGL's market by judgment. Gujarat, meanwhile, is the gas state for a different reason: the terminals, the densest pipeline grid and the factories all sit there.

The real competitor in this kitchen is not a company. It is a price. Every unit a distributor cannot get from the cheap domestic pool must be bought as LNG, at a price set in Qatar and on American export docks. The share of cheap gas in the mix and the landed LNG price are the two cost lines that matter.
c2.read:
Read the five boxes left to right, from the gas field to your stove, then the bands below.

The boxes are the stations: gas source, import terminals, trunk pipelines, city gas network, the customer. Under each you get what happens and who stands there. Notice the names: ONGC and foreign LNG sellers at the source, Petronet and Shell at the terminals, GAIL and GSPL in the pipes, IGL, MGL, Gujarat Gas and Adani Total in the cities, and drivers, households and Morbi kilns at the end.

The band row shows who holds each station. The India listed colour sits only on stations three and four, the trunk pipes and the city networks. The first two stations, where the price of gas is set and where it lands, belong to others. The last station is the customer. That is the visual version of the so-what line: the listed gas utilities do not control the price of what they buy and only partly control the price of what they sell.

The second band row shows where the rival stands, and the rival is unusual: not a foreign company but the imported LNG price, set in Qatar and the US. The row stretches it across the first four stations, from the field to the city network, because LNG is the marginal unit of gas at every one of them. Only the customer station reads World. When that price rises, it presses on every listed station at once.

Use the diagram to trace any headline. A ministry allocation cut enters at station one, as less cheap gas, and lands on station four's margin. A new terminal or pipeline at stations two and three adds volume for the pipe owners. An electric-auto policy enters at station five and travels backwards, as lost CNG demand, to station four.

The note under the boxes names the geography: Gujarat for terminals and industry, Delhi and Mumbai for CNG.

c3.story:
Gas utilities have two volume engines, and they could hardly be more different.

The first is CNG in a handful of big cities. Its customers are auto drivers, taxi fleets, city buses and private car owners, and they choose CNG for one reason: it is cheaper per kilometre than petrol or diesel. At the peak in 2021, CNG cost roughly half as much as petrol for the same running, and conversions boomed. When the discount narrows, after a string of price hikes, drivers stop switching. And now there is a new rival in exactly this fleet: the electric auto and the electric cab, pushed hardest by the same city governments that once pushed CNG.

The second engine is industry, above all Morbi in Gujarat, the town that makes most of India's ceramic tiles. Its kilns burn gas. In 2019 the National Green Tribunal ordered Morbi's polluting coal gasifiers shut, which pushed the cluster onto piped gas. Then in 2022, when the Ukraine war sent LNG to records, kiln owners did the rational thing: they switched to propane, or shut. Industrial gas customers are loyal only to the cheapest fuel of the month.

Around those two engines sit the steadier customers. Households cook on piped gas, which competes with the LPG cylinder. Fertiliser plants use gas as urea feedstock under a pooled price, the biggest single gas consumer and GAIL's anchor volume. Power plants burn gas in heatwaves when the grid is short. Hotels, restaurants and hospitals use it where courts have banned dirtier fuels.

So when someone asks whether gas demand is growing, the honest answer is: which customer? CNG listens to the petrol price and to electric-vehicle policy. Industrial PNG listens to spot LNG and propane. The two can move in opposite directions in the same quarter.
c3.read:
Seven tiles, one per customer group. Each reads in three lines: who buys, what they buy, and what moves them.

The best way to use this grid is to split the tiles by who pays for which gas. Transport CNG and household PNG are the priority customers: under the ministry's rules they get first call on the cheap domestic gas allocation. Industrial PNG and commercial users mostly pay market prices, which in practice means LNG prices. Fertiliser and power plants buy large volumes through the trunk pipelines, so they matter far more to GAIL and GSPL than to the city distributors.

That split tells you which lever moves which tile.

  • The priority tiles are hostage to the allocation notification and to the CNG discount against petrol.
  • The market tiles are hostage to spot LNG against propane and furnace oil.
  • The pipeline tiles follow urea production targets, the fertiliser subsidy budget and summer power shortages.

Then look at the third line of each tile for the threats. Electric vehicles appear on the transport tile, the LPG cylinder on the household tile, propane on the industrial tile. Every distributor tile names a substitute, which you will see again on the five-forces radar in card nine.

The so-what line says the two volume engines are CNG in a few cities and industrial gas in Gujarat. When you open a distributor's results, find out first which of the two it leans on.

c4.story:
A city gas distributor is a chai stall with a ration card. The government allots it a ration of cheap milk, domestic gas at a formula price. Anything beyond the ration it buys at the market rate, imported LNG. The price of chai is its own to set. When the ration is generous, the stall makes a lovely margin. When the ration is cut, the stall either raises the price of chai and watches some customers drift away, or swallows the loss.

That is why the one line that matters most is the gross spread per unit: the selling price minus the gas cost for each unit sold. Running costs are modest: compression power for the CNG stations, network upkeep, staff. Depreciation and interest are small for the old metro distributors, which built their networks long ago and carry almost no debt. What is left is a healthy slice of each rupee, and in a good year EBITDA per unit for the metro names sits in a comfortable band of a few rupees per standard cubic metre.

Two quirks set this industry apart. Working capital barely matters: CNG is sold for cash at the pump, and industry pays on short cycles. And depreciation tells a time-shifted story. A distributor must lay its network before customers arrive, because the licence comes with a minimum build obligation. So a new geographic area runs losses for years, and a company winning lots of new areas, like Adani Total Gas, can look worse on paper while it builds.

Volume growth without margin is how a gas distributor looks busy while earning less.

The pipeline owner's walk is different. Its revenue is the regulator's per-unit tariff times volume; a single tariff order can move profit by a fifth in a day. GAIL then adds a gas-marketing book and polymer plants on top, which bring a commodity swing that a pure pipe would not have.
c4.read:
Two bar charts walk a hundred rupees of sales down to what is left, one for city gas distributors and one for trunk pipelines and marketing. Move left to right on each.

  • The input bar is gas purchased. For the distributor it takes roughly two-thirds of sales. For the second chart it is a little lower, close to three-fifths.
  • The opex bar is compression power, network upkeep and people, around a tenth on both charts.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is small for the distributor and nearly double that for the pipeline door, because long steel pipe is capital heavy.
  • The last bar is what is left: about a seventh for the distributor and about a fifth for the pipeline door.

Two things to notice. First, the second chart's big input bar is not the pipeline itself. It is GAIL's gas-marketing book, where GAIL buys gas and resells it. A pure pipe such as GSPL would show a tiny input bar and a much larger last bar. Second, the distributor keeps less per rupee of sales here yet sits higher on card one's profit bar. That is not a contradiction: a metro distributor earns its slice on a network built long ago and largely paid for, so its return on capital is high, as the cheat sheet in card ten shows.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes; hover a bar for amounts.

In the list below, the gross spread, depreciation, capex and the pipeline tariff get a clear yes. Working capital gets a rare no: gas sells for cash. The so-what asks you to read margin per unit and the cheap-gas share together, every quarter.

c5.story:
For most of a decade, Indian city gas was the boring-but-beautiful corner of the market. Then it found out how much of its beauty was borrowed.

The boom ran from around 2017 to 2021. The regulator held two giant bidding rounds that handed out licences covering most of India's districts. Everyone suddenly had a licence; few had customers yet. Then Covid struck in 2020 and emptied the roads, and CNG volumes collapsed for a quarter. But spot LNG fell to its lowest ever, so the industrial distributors in Gujarat made record margins on what they did sell. By 2021 volumes were back above pre-Covid levels, CNG cost about half as much as petrol to run, and the stocks traded at their richest multiples. Adani's distributor was valued like a technology company.

Then 2022 broke the spell. Russia invaded Ukraine, spot LNG went to records, and the domestic gas price more than doubled under the old formula. CNG prices were raised a dozen times. Morbi's kilns shut. GAIL lost the gas it had contracted from a Russian supplier. In early 2023 the Hindenburg report hit the Adani group, and the technology-company valuation went with it.

The government tried to fix the cost side in 2023 with a new formula pricing domestic gas at a tenth of the crude price, inside a floor and a ceiling. Spreads recovered. And then, in late 2024, the ministry cut the cheap gas allotted to city distributors in two steps, to roughly half of their CNG needs. Prices went up, stocks fell by a third or more, and Delhi's electric-vehicle push started to bite.

In 2026 the picture is a floor, not a launchpad. New LNG from the United States and Qatar is pushing spot prices down, spreads are rebuilding on cheaper imports, and GAIL's new pipelines are lifting transmission volumes. CNG volumes grow in mid single digits. Stabilising, not booming.
c5.read:
Three pieces: the clock, the timeline and four hands.

The clock has four arcs clockwise from the top: boom, peak, bust and bottom. The years under each come from the last lap: a long boom from 2017 to 2021, a peak in 2021, a long bust from 2022 to 2025, and a bottom in 2025 and 2026. The arrow sits just before twelve o'clock, at the very end of the bottom arc and about to cross into boom. The label reads bottoming, LNG glut arriving, and the detail line says spreads have been rebuilt while the cheap-gas share is lower. Hover an arc to read what defined that phase.

The timeline runs from 2019. Read the colours: neutral in 2019 and 2020, boom in 2021, bust in 2022, neutral in 2023 when the new formula helped, bust again in 2024 and 2025 with the allocation cuts, and now in 2026. Notice the bust is a double dip: one caused by the world LNG price, one caused by Delhi.

The four hands tell you whether the arrow keeps moving.

  • Spot LNG in Asia: falling, pointing up. Cheaper imports fill the gap left by lost domestic gas.
  • Domestic gas share in city-gas supply: roughly half, pointing down. The ration was cut and has not come back.
  • CNG discount to petrol: about a third, flat. Not wide enough to drive a conversion wave.
  • Electric-vehicle share in Delhi and Mumbai: rising, pointing down for CNG.

Two hands help, two hurt. That split is why the arrow sits at the cusp rather than inside the boom arc, and why the so-what says the next leg needs cheap LNG to last and the allocation to stay put, neither of which the distributors control.

c6.story:
Ask a city gas CEO what drives the business and you will hear about network expansion, station openings and household connections. Ask the stock and it will tell you about two dials the CEO does not control.

The first is the Asian spot LNG price, quoted off the Japan-Korea Marker. Every unit a distributor buys beyond its domestic allocation is priced off the world LNG market. When spot spikes, as in 2022, margins crash and Morbi's kilns switch to propane or shut. The second is the domestic gas allocation itself, the ration of cheap formula-priced gas the ministry hands out. Raise it and spreads widen overnight; cut it and spreads collapse overnight. Those two together are the distributor's cost of goods.

The third three-dot dial is Brent, and it is two-faced. Domestic gas is priced as a slice of the crude price, inside a floor and a ceiling, so higher crude raises the cost of the cheap gas, at least until the ceiling binds. Many long-term LNG contracts are also linked to crude. But higher crude also raises the petrol price CNG competes against, which widens the discount and helps conversions, if pump prices are allowed to move.

Then come the two-dot dials. A weaker rupee raises the cost of gas bought in dollars. More domestic output from the deep-water fields means more cheap gas to share out. Busy kilns in Gujarat mean industrial volume. And electric-vehicle adoption slowly erodes the CNG fleet. The one-dot dials are slower still: the LPG cylinder price, which decides whether piped kitchen gas looks cheap; urea output, which fills GAIL's pipes; and interest rates, which set the cost of building networks in new areas.
c6.read:
Each row is a dial. Read across: the dial, the channel it travels through, what a rise does, and its weight.

  • The arrow on the rise-does column: green up means a rise helps the industry, red down means it hurts, a diamond means it depends. Only Brent carries a diamond here, for the reason in the story.
  • The weight dots: three for spot LNG, the domestic allocation and Brent. These can make or break a year.

Now look at today's reading column, and notice something striking. The two most important dials, spot LNG and the domestic allocation, both show a dash. Neither has a live series we track. For the very dials that decide the distributors' cost of goods, you have to follow ministry notifications and LNG market news directly.

Where a series exists, read it with care. Brent and the rupee are direct. Domestic gas output maps to the core-sector natural gas index, a fair match. Industrial activity in Gujarat maps to national manufacturing output, a proxy. Electric-vehicle adoption maps to the auto index, a loose proxy. The LPG row maps to housing and fuel inflation, fertiliser to the core fertiliser index, and rates to the money-market rate.

Then count the arrows. Green ups on allocation, domestic output, Gujarat industry, LPG and fertiliser; red downs on spot LNG, the rupee, electric vehicles and rates. The helpful dials are mostly about volume; the harmful ones are mostly about cost. The so-what line tells you to track two dials if you track nothing else: spot LNG and the allocation.

c7.story:
Most of the risks in this industry are slow. One is not, and it matters more than all the others put together.

That one is the cheap gas sitting at the government's discretion. The petroleum ministry decides periodically how much formula-priced domestic gas each city distributor receives. In late 2024, two notifications removed about half of it, and about a third of the sector's market value went with them. There was no demand shock, no accident, no competitor. There was a circular, and a Monday morning repricing.

An allocation notification is a Friday-evening headline that reprices the whole sector by Monday.

Then the slow-burn risks. Electric vehicles are arriving in exactly the fleets that built CNG: autos, cabs and buses in Delhi and Mumbai, which state policies are electrifying first. It will take years, but every electric auto is a CNG customer lost for a decade.

Industrial volume is never really owned. When gas gets dearer, Morbi's kiln owners switch to propane within a month, and switch back when gas gets cheaper. That makes industrial volume cyclical, and it makes Gujarat Gas's quarters much bumpier than IGL's.

Natural gas also sits outside GST, along with crude, petrol, diesel and jet fuel, since GST began in 2017. Industrial buyers cannot claim input credit on it, and state VAT varies widely. A decade of promises to fix this has not delivered.

Laying pipe under Indian cities is its own saga: digging permissions, road restoration charges, slow household conversions. A new area takes about a decade to earn its cost. And old licences are losing their marketing exclusivity, opening the door for rivals to use an incumbent's pipes for a fee, which could one day turn a monopoly margin into a regulated tariff.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck, why it bites, and a severity tag. The tags tell you how to hold each risk in your head.

  • Structural: cheap gas at government discretion, and gas outside GST. These are permanent features. The first sets a ceiling on the multiple the market will pay for any distributor; the second caps industrial demand.
  • Slow: electric vehicles in the CNG cities, and the grind of laying pipe under cities. Real, but measured in years. Use them in your long-term volume assumptions, not your quarterly ones.
  • Cyclical: propane and furnace-oil competition. This one swings with spot LNG, so it rises and falls with the cycle.
  • Two-sided: marketing exclusivity ending. Bad for the incumbent distributor's margin, but potentially good for whoever owns pipes others want to use, and for new entrants.
  • Recurring: dollar cost, rupee price. A rupee slide shows up as a margin hit before a price hike can follow.

Then map the rows to the doors. Almost every row is a distributor risk. The pipeline owner is touched mainly by the GST row, which caps the volume flowing through its pipes. That asymmetry is one reason the call in card eleven leans to the pipeline over the distributors.

The so-what line is blunt: the first row is the one that matters. Set a news alert for ministry allocation notices on every distributor you own.

c8.story:
Delhi's CNG business was not created by a market. It was created by a court. In 1998, hearing a public interest case on the capital's air, the Supreme Court ordered buses, autos and taxis onto CNG. IGL's customers arrived by judgment, and court and pollution-board fuel bans have kept steering users onto gas ever since.

That sets the tone: in gas, the rulebook is the business model. The Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board, PNGRB, decides who may lay pipes in each geographic area, polices the minimum build programme that comes with each licence, and sets the tariffs pipelines charge. For a pipeline owner, the tariff order is revenue. For a distributor, the licence is the moat.

The ministry holds the other big lever, the allocation of domestic gas, with CNG and household piped gas given priority. Next to it sits the price formula, set in 2023 after the Kirit Parikh committee's review: domestic gas at a tenth of the crude price, inside a floor and a slowly rising ceiling, revised monthly. The formula caps the cost of the cheap gas; the allocation decides how much of it you get. One without the other is half a story.

Also in 2023, a unified pipeline tariff replaced pipeline-by-pipeline charges with a single national tariff in a few distance zones. That made gas competitive far from the coast and helped GAIL's volumes.

Two rules are still coming. Open access in city gas, once exclusivity ends, would let rivals ship gas through an incumbent's network for a regulated fee. And the GST Council has long debated bringing natural gas under GST, which would cut costs for industry and lift volumes. Meanwhile state electric-vehicle policies are very much live, quietly eroding the fleet the court once handed to CNG.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or a rule: what it does, why you should care, and its status.

  • Always: PNGRB, the court and pollution-board fuel bans, and state VAT on gas. Permanent fixtures. The VAT row explains why the CNG discount to petrol differs city by city.
  • Live: the ministry's domestic gas allocation, the price formula, the unified pipeline tariff and state electric-vehicle policies. Four live rows is a lot. This is one of the most policy-dense industries on the page, and the live rows are where quarterly earnings get decided.
  • Coming: open access in city gas and the GST question. One is a threat to distributors, the other a gift to everyone.

A useful exercise is to sort the rows by door. The distributors sit under the allocation, the formula, the VAT rows, open access and the EV policies. The pipeline owner sits mainly under PNGRB's tariff powers and the unified tariff, both of which have recently helped it. That lopsided exposure is the regulatory version of the call: more rules can go wrong for the distributors than for the pipe.

Notice too that two rules pull in opposite directions on CNG. The court and pollution bans push users onto gas; the state EV policies pull them off it. Which one wins in a given city decides that city's CNG volume growth.

Dated regulatory news filtered for this industry sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Put a city gas distributor through Porter's five forces and it looks, at first, like a dream. Rivalry is almost nil: each distributor holds a licensed monopoly in its area, and competition happens only once, at the licence auction. New entrants are limited because licences have already been handed out across most of the country, with long exclusivity.

So where does the pressure come from? Look at the supplier. The distributor's suppliers are the government, which sets the price and the quantity of cheap domestic gas, and the world LNG market, which sets the price of everything else. Neither negotiates. That is the full-pressure spoke, and the 2024 allocation cut showed exactly how much it can bite.

Then substitutes. A CNG driver can buy an electric auto. A Morbi kiln can burn propane. A household can stay on the LPG cylinder. Every customer group a distributor serves has an alternative, which is why buyers also carry real power: CNG drivers compare with petrol daily and industry compares with propane monthly.

The distributor's monopoly is real. It is a monopoly over the pipe, not over the customer's choice of fuel.

The pipeline's shape is much calmer. Its users are locked in by geography: if your fertiliser plant is on GAIL's line, you are not switching pipes. The pipeline does not own the gas, it simply passes it through, so supplier power is modest. Entrants are the weakest force of all; nobody builds a parallel trunk line next to an existing one. The only real substitute for a pipeline is not moving gas at all.

The so-what puts it neatly: since 2024 the market has started to price the distributors' margin as a policy gift that can be withdrawn, and the pipeline's regulated, steadier slice as the safer one.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes: rivalry at the top, then clockwise supplier power, buyer power, new entrants and substitutes. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure that force puts on the business. A smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn: city gas distributors and trunk pipelines. Start with the overall size. The distributors' shape is clearly larger, and it is lopsided: it reaches the outer ring on supplier power at a full three, and nearly so on substitutes at two and a half, with buyer power at two. On rivalry both shapes sit at one, so they overlap at the top: neither door competes much day to day.

The pipeline's shape is small and roundish: a little over one on supplier power and substitutes, one on buyer power, and just half a point on entrants, the tightest spoke on the chart. That is the geometry of a toll road.

Now find the gap between the shapes. It is widest on supplier power and on substitutes. Those two spokes are the distributor's two worries, the government's ration and the electric auto, and neither applies much to the pipe.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero to three with a reason. If you own a specific distributor, adjust its shape in your head: an industrial-heavy Gujarat distributor would push further out on buyer and substitute power because kilns switch to propane, while a metro CNG name would push out on substitutes as electric vehicles spread.

c10.story:
A city gas results call can sound complicated: volumes in million standard cubic metres per day, APM share, price revisions, new geographic areas, CNG station counts. Eight numbers make it simple.

Begin with EBITDA per unit of gas sold, the distributor's one number. For the metro names it has lived in a band of a few rupees per standard cubic metre, and the market watches every quarter's move within that band. A fall of a rupee is a bad quarter. Then split volume growth into CNG and industrial, because the two engines answer to different signals. CNG growing in mid single digits is healthy for a mature city; industrial volume is positive only when spot LNG is cheap enough to beat propane.

Next, the cost structure. Gross margin tells you the gap between selling price and gas cost before running costs. The domestic gas share of CNG supply tells you how exposed the mix is to LNG, and it comes with a handy rule of thumb in the table: each tenth of supply lost from the cheap pool needs a price hike of roughly two rupees a kilogram to hold margins.

Then the build. Capex to depreciation shows how hard a company is extending its network. For a metro distributor, moderate is right; for a company racing into new areas with few customers yet, a very high ratio is a warning that it is building ahead of demand. For the pipeline owner, transmission volume is the revenue driver, rising with each new fertiliser or power connection.

Finally, the scorecard. Return on capital shows whether a decade of digging earns its keep: the metro distributors historically earn far more than pipelines and new areas. And net debt to EBITDA shows how much of the new-area build is on borrowed money.
c10.read:
One row per number: what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median from the listed companies' latest filings.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask on every results call.
  • What good looks like gives the rules of thumb: EBITDA of six to eight rupees per standard cubic metre for metro distributors, CNG volume growth in mid to high single digits, gross margin above three-tenths of sales, a domestic gas share above half, capex at one and a half to two and a half times depreciation while volumes grow, and return on capital above a fifth for the metro names. These are benchmarks, not targets.
  • Today's industry median appears where the number maps to a standard filing line.

Three rows will show a dash: EBITDA per unit, domestic gas share and pipeline transmission volume. These come from company presentations and ministry data, not standard financial statements, so no median can be computed. The volume-growth row shows a sales-growth median, which is revenue, not volume. In a year of price hikes, revenue growth flatters volume growth, so read it with that in mind.

The medians also blend two doors and companies at very different stages, from debt-free metro distributors to network builders. Compare any one company against the good-looks-like column for its own door first, then glance at the median for context.

The quickest single check: take a distributor's EBITDA per unit this quarter, compare it with the band, then look at its domestic gas share. Margin and mix together tell you most of the story.

c11.story:
Gas utilities give you a mix of instant news and slow warnings, and the trick is to treat them differently.

The instant news comes from two sources. Ministry allocation notifications change the cheap-gas share from the next billing cycle, so their effect lands in the same quarter. PNGRB tariff orders reprice a pipeline's revenue from the date of the order. Neither gives you advance warning, but both deserve an immediate reaction.

The one-quarter signals are where most of the forecasting happens. Spot LNG bought today is sold next quarter, so the spot price is next quarter's cost. Petrol and diesel pump prices set the CNG discount, which drives conversions a quarter later. Morbi's ceramic exports and kiln utilisation tell you whether Gujarat's industrial volume will hold. And a new pipeline or terminal commissioned now, say a fertiliser plant connected to GAIL's grid, is a step up in transmission volume next quarter.

The slowest signals are two quarters out, and they are about the long game: electric auto and cab registrations in Delhi and Mumbai, each one a CNG customer lost for a decade, and output from the deep-water fields, because more domestic gas means more to allot, or at least no further cuts.

Now the rule. The industry is in an up-cycle when spot LNG is falling, the domestic allocation is stable or rising, and the CNG discount to petrol is widening. Today two signs are on. LNG is falling as the supply wave arrives, and the allocation is stable, with no new cuts but no restoration either. The CNG discount, though, has narrowed after the price hikes. Two of three means spreads are rebuilding, which is exactly what the clock showed. The call follows: prefer the pipeline owner, whose tariff is regulated and whose volumes are rising, and among distributors, prefer industrial exposure as cheap LNG arrives.

The chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot to read the channel through which it reaches earnings.

Read the dots in three groups.

  • Same quarter, on the left: ministry allocation notifications and PNGRB tariff orders. These are not forecasts; they are events. When one appears, the quarter has already changed.
  • One quarter ahead, in the middle: spot LNG, pump prices, Morbi kilns and new pipeline connections. This is your main reading list each quarter.
  • Two quarters ahead, on the right: electric-vehicle registrations and deep-water gas output. These shape the long-run volume story more than any one quarter.

Below the chart, the rule shows three signs. Spot LNG falling has a tick, with the note supply wave arriving. Domestic allocation stable has a tick, with the note no new cuts, no restoration. CNG discount widening has a cross: it narrowed after price hikes. Two ticks match the rule's middle reading, spreads rebuilding.

Then the call box: the headline, three points, and what would change the call. The three would-change items are your alert list: a restoration of the domestic allocation, which would be an instant re-rating; a spot LNG spike from a Middle East or shipping shock; and gas brought under GST. Notice that the first and third are policy events, which is fitting for an industry where the rulebook has done more damage, and could do more good, than the market.
